tips.content: To find the area under a curve that isn't a simple triangle or rectangle, you can count the squares on the graph paper. Multiply the number of squares by the 'value' of one square (width in $s$ $	imes$ height in $m/s$).

questions.q: What is the key difference between a distance-time graph and a displacement-time graph?

opts.B: Displacement-time graphs can have negative values

questions.exp: The answer is B. Since displacement is a vector, it can be negative (indicating a position in the opposite direction from the origin). Distance is always positive.

questions.q: What does a negative gradient on a displacement-time graph represent?

opts.B: The object is moving backwards (towards or past the origin)

questions.exp: The answer is B. The gradient of a displacement-time graph is velocity. A negative gradient means a negative velocity, indicating movement in the opposite direction.

questions.q: On a velocity-time graph, what does the area 'below' the x-axis (negative velocity) represent?
questions.exp: The answer is B. Area represents displacement. If the velocity is negative, the area is negative, meaning the object is returning towards the starting point.

questions.q: If a velocity-time graph is a straight line with a negative gradient, the acceleration is:
questions.exp: The answer is B. A straight line has a constant gradient. Since it is sloping downwards, the gradient (acceleration) is negative.

questions.q: A runner's displacement-time graph is a straight line from $(0,0)$ to $(10\,s, -20\,m)$. What is their velocity?
questions.exp: The correct answer is -2. Velocity = gradient = $(-20 - 0) / (10 - 0) = -2\,m/s$.

questions.q: How do you calculate total displacement from a velocity-time graph that goes above and below the x-axis?

opts.A: Add all areas together as positive values
opts.B: Subtract the area below the axis from the area above the axis
opts.C: Only use the area above the axis
opts.D: Find the gradient of the whole graph

questions.exp: The answer is B. Displacement is a vector. To find the resultant displacement, you must treat areas above the axis as positive and areas below as negative.

questions.q: A ball is thrown up and caught at the same height. Which velocity-time graph best describes this (taking up as positive)?

opts.A: A horizontal line above the x-axis
opts.B: A straight line with a negative gradient crossing the x-axis
opts.C: A straight line with a positive gradient starting at zero
opts.D: A curve that stays above the x-axis

questions.exp: The answer is B. The ball starts with positive velocity, decreases to zero at the top (crosses x-axis), and then has an increasing negative velocity as it falls. The gradient is constant $-g$.

questions.q: What is the acceleration of an object if its velocity-time graph is $v = 5t + 2$?
questions.exp: The correct answer is 5. Comparing $v = 5t + 2$ to $y = mx + c$, the gradient $m$ (acceleration) is 5.

questions.q: If an object's displacement-time graph is a parabola ($s \propto t^2$), the velocity is:
questions.exp: The answer is B. If $s = kt^2$, then velocity (the derivative/gradient) is $v = 2kt$. This shows velocity is proportional to time, meaning it increases linearly.

questions.q: An object moves at $+5\,m/s$ for $2\,s$ and then $-5\,m/s$ for $2\,s$. What is its total distance travelled?
questions.exp: The correct answer is 20. Distance is a scalar. Total distance = $(5 	imes 2) + (5 	imes 2) = 10 + 10 = 20\,m$. (Note: Displacement would be 0).

tips.content: In exams, check the axes carefully! A common mistake is using the rules for a velocity-time graph on a displacement-time graph. Remember: gradient of s-t is velocity; area of v-t is displacement.

title: Tricky points on s-t and v-t graphs

questions.q: When an object changes direction, what happens on a velocity-time graph?
questions.exp: The answer is B. To change direction, velocity must pass through zero as it changes from positive to negative (or vice versa).

questions.q: What does a 'sharp corner' (discontinuity in gradient) on a velocity-time graph imply?
questions.exp: The answer is A. Since the gradient is acceleration, a sudden change in gradient means the acceleration changed instantly (e.g., during a collision).

questions.q: A bouncing ball's velocity-time graph shows a vertical line jumping from negative to positive. What does this represent?

opts.A: The ball at its maximum height

questions.exp: The answer is B. During a bounce, the velocity changes from negative (downwards) to positive (upwards) almost instantly.

questions.q: How is 'instantaneous acceleration' found from a curved velocity-time graph?

opts.A: Dividing final velocity by total time
opts.B: Finding the area under the curve
opts.C: Drawing a tangent to the curve and finding its gradient
opts.D: Connecting the start and end points with a straight line

questions.exp: The answer is C. The gradient at a specific point on a curve is found by drawing a tangent at that point.

questions.q: If a displacement-time graph is a horizontal line at $s = 5\,m$, what is the velocity at $t = 10\,s$?
questions.exp: The correct answer is 0. A horizontal line on an s-t graph means the object is stationary, so velocity is zero.

questions.q: Why is the gradient of a displacement-time graph for a falling object NOT constant?

opts.B: The object is accelerating, so velocity is changing
opts.D: The mass of the object changes

questions.exp: The answer is B. Because the object accelerates, its velocity (the gradient) must increase over time, resulting in a curve.

questions.q: What is the displacement of an object that moves $10\,m$ Right and then $10\,m$ Left?
questions.exp: The answer is C. Displacement is a vector. $+10 + (-10) = 0\,m$.

questions.q: In a real-world v-t graph for a car, why are the corners usually 'rounded' rather than sharp?

opts.A: The car cannot change acceleration infinitely fast
opts.C: The speed of light is a limit

questions.exp: The answer is A. Changing acceleration (known as 'jerk') takes time. You can't go from $0$ to full acceleration instantly; the foot must move the pedal.

questions.q: If the area under a velocity-time graph is $50\,m$ above the axis and $20\,m$ below the axis, what is the total distance?
questions.exp: The correct answer is 70. For distance, we sum the magnitudes of all movements regardless of direction: $50 + 20 = 70\,m$.

questions.q: Which of the following are true for an object at its maximum height when thrown upwards? (Select all that apply)

opts.D: The displacement-time graph has a gradient of zero

questions.exp: The correct options are A, C, and D. Gravity (acceleration) always acts, even when the object is momentarily stationary at the top. Since $v=0$, the gradient of the s-t graph is zero.

tips.content: For a bouncing ball, the v-t graph looks like a series of parallel lines. The lines are parallel because the acceleration (gradient) is always $g = -9.81\,m/s^2$ while the ball is in the air.

questions.q: Under what specific condition can the SUVAT equations be used?
questions.exp: The answer is B. SUVAT equations (equations of motion) only apply when the acceleration of the object is uniform (constant).

questions.q: What does the 's' represent in SUVAT?
questions.exp: The correct answer is displacement. It is a vector quantity representing the change in position, not just the total distance traveled.

questions.q: Which equation relates final velocity, initial velocity, acceleration, and time?
questions.exp: The answer is C. This is the definition of acceleration rearranged: $a = (v-u)/t$ becomes $v = u + at$.

questions.q: An object starts from rest and accelerates at $2\,m/s^2$ for $5\,s$. What is its final velocity?
questions.exp: The answer is C. $u=0, a=2, t=5$. $v = u + at = 0 + (2 \times 5) = 10\,m/s$.

questions.q: A car decelerates from $20\,m/s$ to $5\,m/s$ in $3\,s$. What is its acceleration? (Include sign)
Which SUVAT equation does NOT contain the variable 't'?
questions.exp: The answer is C. This equation is useful when the time for the motion is unknown.

questions.q: A ball is thrown upwards with initial velocity $u$. At its maximum height, what is its velocity $v$?
questions.exp: The answer is C. At the peak of its trajectory, an object momentarily stops before falling back down, so $v = 0$.

questions.q: If a stone is dropped from a cliff, what value should be used for acceleration 'a' (assuming no air resistance)?
questions.exp: The correct answer is $9.81\,m/s^2$ (the acceleration due to gravity). In some exam boards, $9.8$ is used, but AQA standard is $9.81$.

questions.q: Which of the following are vector quantities? Select all that apply.
questions.exp: The correct options are A, C and D. Displacement, velocity, and acceleration all have direction. Time is a scalar quantity.

questions.q: A runner accelerates from $4\,m/s$ to $8\,m/s$ over a distance of $12\,m$. What is their acceleration?
questions.exp: The answer is A. Using $v^2 = u^2 + 2as \rightarrow 8^2 = 4^2 + 2(a)(12) \rightarrow 64 = 16 + 24a \rightarrow 48 = 24a \rightarrow a = 2\,m/s^2$.

tips.content: Sign convention is vital! Always decide which direction is positive (e.g., upwards = +). If gravity acts downwards, use $a = -9.81\,m/s^2$. If the object ends up below its starting point, displacement $s$ will be negative.
When solving problems, list your 'knowns' and 'unknowns' for S, U, V, A, T. Pick the equation that contains the three things you know and the one thing you want to find.

questions.q: The first SUVAT equation ($v = u + at$) is derived from the definition of which quantity?
questions.exp: The answer is C. Acceleration is defined as the rate of change of velocity: $a = \Delta v / t = (v-u)/t$.

questions.q: What feature of a velocity-time graph represents the displacement of the object?
questions.exp: The answer is B. Integrating velocity with respect to time (calculating the area) gives the total displacement.

questions.q: A velocity-time graph for constant acceleration is a straight line. What shape is formed between the line and the time axis (from $t=0$ to $t$)?
questions.exp: The correct answer is a Trapezium. The area of this trapezium represents displacement: $s = \frac{u+v}{2}t$.

questions.q: When deriving $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$ from a $v-t$ graph, the area is split into a rectangle and a triangle. What is the height of the triangle?
questions.exp: The answer is C. The triangle sits on top of a rectangle of height $u$. Since the total height is $v$, the triangle's height is $v - u$.

questions.q: In the derivation of $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$, what is substituted for $(v - u)$?
questions.exp: The answer is B. From $v = u + at$, we know $(v - u) = at$. Substituting this into the triangle area $\frac{1}{2}(v-u)t$ gives $\frac{1}{2}(at)t = \frac{1}{2}at^2$.

questions.q: To derive $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$, which variable is eliminated from the other equations?
questions.exp: The correct answer is time ($t$). By rearranging $v = u + at$ to $t = (v-u)/a$ and substituting it into $s = \frac{u+v}{2}t$, the time variable is removed.

questions.q: What does the gradient of a displacement-time graph represent?
questions.exp: The answer is A. The rate of change of displacement is velocity ($v = ds/dt$).

questions.q: What does the gradient of a velocity-time graph represent?
questions.exp: The answer is C. The rate of change of velocity is acceleration ($a = dv/dt$).

questions.q: Which of these are valid SUVAT equations? Select all that apply.
questions.exp: The correct options are A, B and C. Option D is incorrect; it should be $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$.

questions.q: Write the SUVAT equation that relates displacement, final velocity, acceleration, and time (omitting 'u').
questions.exp: The correct answer is $s = vt - \frac{1}{2}at^2$. This is derived by substituting $u = v - at$ into the area equation.

tips.content: A-Level exams often ask you to 'Show that...' or 'Derive...'. For SUVAT, always start by sketching a velocity-time graph showing a constant gradient starting at $u$ and ending at $v$ over time $t$. The area and gradient of this graph are your starting points.
Graph analysis summary: Displacement-time gradient = Velocity. Velocity-time gradient = Acceleration. Velocity-time area = Displacement. Acceleration-time area = Change in velocity.

questions.q: A car accelerates from $10\,m/s$ to $30\,m/s$ in $4\,s$. How far does it travel?
questions.exp: The answer is B. $u=10, v=30, t=4$. $s = \frac{u+v}{2}t = \frac{10+30}{2} \times 4 = 20 \times 4 = 80\,m$.

questions.q: An arrow is fired vertically upwards at $40\,m/s$. How long does it take to reach its maximum height?
questions.exp: The answer is B. $u=40, v=0, a=-9.81$. $v = u + at \rightarrow 0 = 40 - 9.81t \rightarrow t = 40/9.81 \approx 4.08\,s$.

questions.q: A ball is dropped from a height of $20\,m$. With what speed does it hit the ground? (Assume $g = 9.81\,m/s^2$)
A particle starts from rest and travels $100\,m$ with a constant acceleration of $5\,m/s^2$. How long did this take?
questions.exp: The answer is A. $u=0, s=100, a=5$. $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2 \rightarrow 100 = 0 + 2.5t^2 \rightarrow t^2 = 40 \rightarrow t \approx 6.32\,s$.

questions.q: A car traveling at $15\,m/s$ brakes to a stop over $30\,m$. What is the magnitude of the deceleration?
questions.exp: The answer is B. $u=15, v=0, s=30$. $v^2 = u^2 + 2as \rightarrow 0 = 15^2 + 2a(30) \rightarrow 0 = 225 + 60a \rightarrow a = -225/60 = -3.75\,m/s^2$. Magnitude is $3.75$.

questions.q: A plane lands at $60\,m/s$ and decelerates at $3\,m/s^2$. What is the minimum runway length required?
questions.exp: The correct answer is $600\,m$. $u=60, v=0, a=-3$. $v^2 = u^2 + 2as \rightarrow 0 = 3600 - 6s \rightarrow 6s = 3600 \rightarrow s = 600\,m$.

questions.q: A ball is thrown down from a bridge with initial speed $5\,m/s$. After $2\,s$, what is its velocity?
An object travels $50\,m$ in $5\,s$ while accelerating. If its final velocity is $15\,m/s$, what was its initial velocity?
questions.exp: The answer is B. $s=50, t=5, v=15$. $s = \frac{u+v}{2}t \rightarrow 50 = \frac{u+15}{2} \times 5 \rightarrow 10 = \frac{u+15}{2} \rightarrow 20 = u+15 \rightarrow u = 5\,m/s$.

questions.q: A projectile is launched. Which of these remain constant during its flight (ignore air resistance)? Select all that apply.
questions.exp: The correct options are A and C. Horizontal velocity is constant because there's no horizontal force. Vertical acceleration is constant ($g = 9.81$). Vertical velocity and total speed change throughout the flight.

questions.q: Calculate the total time in the air for a ball thrown upwards at $15\,m/s$ that returns to the same height.
questions.exp: The correct answer is $3.06\,s$. $u=15, s=0, a=-9.81$. $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2 \rightarrow 0 = 15t - 4.905t^2 \rightarrow 15 = 4.905t \rightarrow t \approx 3.06\,s$.

tips.content: For vertical motion: 'Maximum height' means $v=0$. 'Total time in flight' for a return to start means $s=0$. 'Time to peak' is exactly half of 'Total time' if the launch and landing heights are the same.
Always check your units! If speed is in $km/h$, you must convert to $m/s$ by dividing by $3.6$ before using SUVAT equations.

questions.q: What is the correct relationship for total stopping distance?
questions.exp: The answer is B. Total stopping distance is the sum of the distance traveled during the reaction time (thinking distance) and the distance traveled while the brakes are applied (braking distance).

questions.q: How does thinking distance relate to the initial speed $v$ of the vehicle?
questions.exp: The answer is A. Thinking distance is $v \times t_{reaction}$. Since reaction time is roughly constant, distance is directly proportional to speed.

questions.q: How does braking distance relate to the initial speed $v$ of the vehicle?
questions.exp: The answer is B. From $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$, setting $v=0$ gives $s = u^2 / 2a$. For a constant braking force, the braking distance is proportional to the square of the speed.

questions.q: A driver has a reaction time of $0.7\,s$. If they are traveling at $20\,m/s$, what is their thinking distance?
questions.exp: The correct answer is $14\,m$. $d = v \times t = 20 \times 0.7 = 14\,m$.

questions.q: Which of these factors specifically increases the thinking distance?
questions.exp: The answer is C. Thinking distance is determined by the driver's reaction time. Tiredness, alcohol, and distractions increase reaction time. The other options affect the braking distance.

questions.q: If the speed of a car doubles, what happens to the braking distance?
questions.exp: The answer is C. Since braking distance is proportional to $v^2$, doubling the speed ($2v$) results in $2^2 = 4$ times the distance.

questions.q: A car stops in $50\,m$. If its thinking distance was $15\,m$, what was its braking distance?
questions.exp: The correct answer is $35\,m$. $\text{Stopping} = \text{Thinking} + \text{Braking} \rightarrow 50 = 15 + \text{Braking} \rightarrow \text{Braking} = 35\,m$.

questions.q: Why does an icy road increase stopping distance?

opts.A: It increases the driver's reaction time
opts.C: It reduces the friction/adhesion between tires and road

questions.exp: The answer is C. Less friction means a lower maximum deceleration 'a'. From $s = u^2 / 2a$, a smaller 'a' leads to a larger braking distance 's'.

questions.q: Which of the following factors increase the braking distance? Select all that apply.
questions.exp: The correct options are A, B and D. Higher speed and mass increase kinetic energy, requiring more distance to dissipate. Wet roads reduce friction. Caffeine might *decrease* thinking distance by speeding up reactions, but doesn't affect the car's mechanics.

questions.q: A car decelerates at $6\,m/s^2$. Calculate the braking distance from an initial speed of $30\,m/s$.
questions.exp: The correct answer is $75\,m$. $u=30, v=0, a=-6$. $v^2 = u^2 + 2as \rightarrow 0 = 900 - 12s \rightarrow 12s = 900 \rightarrow s = 75\,m$.

tips.content: Be careful with 'Speed vs Distance' relationships. Thinking distance is linear ($s \propto v$). Braking distance is quadratic ($s \propto v^2$). This is why speed limits in residential areas are so strictly enforced—a small increase in speed leads to a much larger stopping distance.

When discussing factors, keep them separate! Thinking = Driver (Brain). Braking = Car/Road (Physics). Don't say 'rain increases reaction time'—it doesn't, it increases braking distance by reducing friction.

questions.q: From a physics perspective, how do features like crumple zones and airbags protect passengers?

opts.A: They increase the force of impact
opts.B: They decrease the time of impact
opts.C: They increase the time of impact

questions.exp: The answer is C. $F = \Delta p / t$. By increasing the time ($t$) it takes for the passenger to come to a stop, the rate of change of momentum is reduced, resulting in a smaller impact force ($F$).

questions.q: Which part of a car is designed to deform plastically during a collision to absorb energy?
questions.exp: The answer is B. Crumple zones at the front and rear are designed to crush. This work done in deforming the metal absorbs kinetic energy that would otherwise be transferred to the passengers.

questions.q: State the equation that relates force, change in momentum, and time.
questions.exp: The correct answer is $F = \Delta p / t$ (or $F = ma$). This shows that force is inversely proportional to the time taken for a change in momentum to occur.

questions.q: A passenger's momentum changes by $1200\,kg\,m/s$ during a crash. If the airbag increases the stopping time from $0.05\,s$ to $0.2\,s$, what is the new average force?
questions.exp: The answer is B. $F = \Delta p / t = 1200 / 0.2 = 6000\,N$. Without the airbag, it would have been $1200 / 0.05 = 24000\,N$.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of a seatbelt?

opts.A: To stop the passenger from moving at all
opts.B: To increase the stopping time and prevent the passenger hitting the dashboard
opts.C: To make the car more aerodynamic

questions.exp: The answer is B. Seatbelts stretch slightly to increase the time taken for the person to stop and keep them secured so they decelerate with the car rather than flying forward into hard surfaces.

questions.q: Why is it important that the passenger cell (the middle of the car) does NOT crumple?
accepted_answers: To protect the occupants from being crushed
questions.exp: The correct answer is to protect occupants from being crushed. While the ends of the car should deform to absorb energy, the survival space around the passengers must remain intact.

questions.q: What happens to the kinetic energy of a car during a crash?

opts.B: It is converted into potential energy
opts.C: It is converted into heat and sound, and work is done deforming the car
opts.D: It is stored in the battery

questions.exp: The answer is C. Energy is conserved. In a crash, the KE is transferred into thermal energy (heat), sound energy, and the work done to permanently deform the car's structure.

questions.q: Which safety feature helps prevent the 'whiplash' injury by limiting the movement of the head relative to the torso?
questions.exp: The answer is B. Headrests support the head during a rear-end collision, ensuring the head accelerates at the same rate as the rest of the body, preventing neck strain.

questions.q: Which of these are intended effects of safety features during a collision? Select all that apply.

opts.A: Decrease the rate of change of momentum
opts.C: Spread the force over a larger surface area

questions.exp: The correct options are A and C. Decreasing the rate of change of momentum reduces force. Airbags also spread the force over the passenger's whole torso/face rather than just a narrow seatbelt strap, reducing pressure ($P=F/A$).

questions.q: If an impact force is $5000\,N$ and acts for $0.15\,s$, what is the impulse delivered to the passenger?
questions.exp: The correct answer is $750\,Ns$. Impulse = Force $\times$ Time = $5000 \times 0.15 = 750\,Ns$ (which is equal to the change in momentum).

tips.content: The mantra for safety questions is: 'Increase the time of impact, decrease the rate of change of momentum, decrease the force.' Use these exact phrases in your written answers for maximum marks.

Work Done = Force $\times$ Distance. Crumple zones allow the car to stop over a longer distance ($s$). Since $W = \Delta KE$ is constant for a given speed, a larger $s$ results in a smaller average Force $F$.

questions.q: What is the key assumption made about the horizontal and vertical components of projectile motion?

opts.A: They are dependent on each other
opts.B: They are independent of each other

questions.exp: The answer is B. In projectile motion, the horizontal and vertical components of motion are independent. This allows us to solve for each dimension separately using SUVAT equations.

questions.q: In the absence of air resistance, what is the horizontal acceleration ($a_x$) of a projectile?
questions.exp: The answer is C. Because there are no horizontal forces acting on the projectile (ignoring air resistance), the horizontal acceleration is zero, and horizontal velocity remains constant.

questions.q: State the value of vertical acceleration ($a_y$) used for a projectile in free fall near Earth's surface.
questions.exp: The correct answer is $-9.81 ms^{-2}$. This is the acceleration due to gravity ($g$). By convention, downwards is usually taken as negative in projectile calculations.

questions.q: A ball is projected horizontally from a height. How does the time taken to hit the ground compare to a ball dropped vertically from the same height?

opts.C: They take the same amount of time
opts.D: It depends on the horizontal speed

questions.exp: The answer is C. Since horizontal and vertical motions are independent, and both start with an initial vertical velocity of $0 ms^{-1}$, they will fall the same vertical distance in the same time.

questions.q: If a ball is projected horizontally at $15 ms^{-1}$ from a height of $20 m$, what is its initial vertical velocity ($u_y$)?
questions.exp: The answer is B. Horizontal projection implies that all the initial velocity is in the x-direction, meaning the initial vertical velocity is zero.

questions.q: Which SUVAT equation is most commonly used to find the time of flight for a horizontally projected object if the height ($s_y$) is known?
questions.exp: The answer is C. Using $s_y = u_y t + 1/2 a_y t^2$ with $u_y = 0$ simplifies to $s_y = 1/2 a_y t^2$, which is the most direct way to solve for time $t$.

questions.q: A stone is thrown horizontally at $10 ms^{-1}$ and takes $2.0 s$ to hit the ground. Calculate the horizontal distance (range) it travels.
questions.exp: The correct answer is $20 m$. For horizontal motion, $s_x = v_x \times t$. So, $10 ms^{-1} \times 2.0 s = 20 m$.

questions.q: What happens to the vertical velocity of a projectile as it falls?
questions.exp: The answer is B. Due to the constant acceleration of gravity ($g$), the vertical velocity increases in the downward direction over time ($v_y = u_y + gt$).

questions.q: If air resistance were included, how would the range of the projectile change?

opts.C: The range would stay the same
opts.D: The trajectory would become perfectly symmetrical

questions.exp: The answer is B. Air resistance provides a decelerating force in both the horizontal and vertical directions, reducing both the time of flight and the horizontal velocity, leading to a shorter range.

questions.q: Identify the shape of the path followed by a projectile under the influence of gravity alone.
questions.exp: The correct answer is a parabola. The combination of constant horizontal velocity and constant vertical acceleration creates a quadratic relationship between $y$ and $x$ displacements.

tips.content: When solving projectile problems, always start by splitting your page into two columns: 'Horizontal' and 'Vertical'. List your SUVAT variables for each separately. Remember: $a_x = 0$ and $a_y = -9.81 ms^{-2}$. The only variable that connects the two columns is time ($t$).

questions.q: When a projectile is launched at an angle $\theta$ to the horizontal with velocity $U$, what is the initial horizontal component ($u_x$)?
questions.exp: The answer is B. Using trigonometry on the velocity vector, the side adjacent to the angle is the horizontal component, so $u_x = U \cos\theta$.

questions.q: What is the initial vertical velocity component ($u_y$) for a projectile launched at angle $\theta$ with velocity $U$?
questions.exp: The answer is B. The vertical component is the side opposite the angle in the velocity vector triangle, so $u_y = U \sin\theta$.

questions.q: At the maximum height of a projectile's trajectory, what is the value of the vertical velocity ($v_y$)?
questions.exp: The answer is C. At the very peak of the flight, the projectile momentarily stops moving upwards before it begins to fall, so $v_y = 0$.

questions.q: A football is kicked at $20 ms^{-1}$ at an angle of $30^{\circ}$ to the horizontal. Calculate its initial vertical velocity.
questions.exp: The correct answer is $10 ms^{-1}$. $u_y = U \sin\theta = 20 \times \sin(30^{\circ}) = 20 \times 0.5 = 10 ms^{-1}$.

questions.q: A projectile is launched from ground level and returns to ground level. If the time to reach maximum height is $T$, what is the total time of flight?
questions.exp: The answer is C. Due to the symmetry of the parabolic path (ignoring air resistance), the time taken to go up to the peak is exactly equal to the time taken to come back down.

questions.q: Which angle of projection (measured from the horizontal) results in the maximum horizontal range?
questions.exp: The answer is B. $45^{\circ}$ provides the optimal balance between initial horizontal velocity and time of flight, resulting in the furthest range.

questions.q: A projectile has a total time of flight of $6.0 s$. How long did it take to reach its maximum height?
questions.exp: The correct answer is $3.0 s$. In a symmetrical flight, the time to reach the peak is half of the total time of flight.

questions.q: Does the horizontal velocity component change during the flight of a projectile launched at an angle?

opts.A: Yes, it decreases as it goes up
opts.B: Yes, it increases as it goes down
opts.D: It becomes zero at the peak

questions.exp: The answer is C. Just like horizontal projection, there are no horizontal forces acting, so $v_x = u_x$ throughout the entire flight.

questions.q: Calculate the horizontal component of velocity for a shell fired at $100 ms^{-1}$ at an angle of $60^{\circ}$ to the horizontal.
questions.exp: The answer is A. $u_x = U \cos\theta = 100 \times \cos(60^{\circ}) = 100 \times 0.5 = 50 ms^{-1}$.

questions.q: Which of the following are true at the peak of a projectile's path? (Select all that apply)
questions.exp: The correct options are A and C. At the peak, $v_y = 0$, but the object still has its constant horizontal velocity $v_x$. The acceleration is constant gravity ($9.81 ms^{-2}$ downwards) throughout the flight.

tips.content: Remember SOH CAH TOA for resolving vectors. $U_y$ is 'Opposite' the angle, so use Sine ($U \sin\theta$). $U_x$ is 'Adjacent' to the angle, so use Cosine ($U \cos\theta$). A common mistake is swapping these!

questions.q: A ball is launched from a height of $2 m$ above the ground at an angle. To find the time of flight, what should be the value of vertical displacement ($s_y$) when it hits the ground?
questions.exp: The answer is B. If we take the launch point as $0$, the ground is $2 m$ below the starting position, so the displacement is $-2 m$.

questions.q: When a projectile is launched and lands at a different height, is the trajectory symmetrical?

opts.D: Only if the landing is higher than the launch

questions.exp: The answer is B. Symmetry only applies when the launch and landing heights are the same. If they differ, the time spent ascending is not equal to the time spent descending.

questions.q: If a projectile is launched from a cliff, at what point does it have its maximum speed?

opts.B: At the peak of the trajectory
opts.C: Just before it hits the ground

questions.exp: The answer is C. Total velocity is the vector sum of $v_x$ and $v_y$. Since $v_x$ is constant and $v_y$ increases as it falls below the launch height, the speed is greatest at the lowest point.

questions.q: Define 'displacement' in the context of projectile motion.
accepted_answers: The straight-line distance and direction from the start point
questions.exp: The correct answer is the straight-line distance from the starting point to the final position, including direction. It is a vector quantity.

questions.q: An object is thrown upwards at an angle. During the descent phase (after the peak), what is the sign of $v_y$ if upwards is positive?
questions.exp: The answer is B. Once the object passes the peak and moves downwards, its velocity vector points in the negative direction.

questions.q: How do you calculate the actual speed $v$ of a projectile if you know $v_x$ and $v_y$?
questions.exp: The answer is B. Velocity is a vector. To find the magnitude (speed), you use Pythagoras' theorem on the horizontal and vertical components.

questions.q: A ball is thrown from a $10 m$ balcony. At what height is its vertical displacement $s_y = 0$?
questions.exp: The answer is B. Displacement is measured from the starting point. Therefore, $s_y = 0$ when the ball is at the same vertical level as where it was thrown.

questions.q: A projectile is launched with $u_x = 12 ms^{-1}$ and $u_y = 5 ms^{-1}$. Calculate its initial launch speed.
questions.exp: The correct answer is $13 ms^{-1}$. Using Pythagoras: $U = \sqrt{12^2 + 5^2} = \sqrt{144 + 25} = \sqrt{169} = 13 ms^{-1}$.

questions.q: When using the quadratic formula to solve $s = ut + 1/2 at^2$ for time, what does a negative time value usually represent physically?

opts.B: The time the object would have been at that height if the trajectory started earlier

questions.exp: The answer is B. Mathematically, the parabola exists for all time. A negative result is a 'virtual' solution representing where the particle would have been before $t=0$ to follow that same curve.

questions.q: If a projectile is launched horizontally from a cliff of height $H$, which expression gives the time to hit the ground?
questions.exp: The answer is B. From $s = 1/2 at^2$, we get $H = 1/2 g t^2$. Rearranging for $t$ gives $t = \sqrt{2H/g}$.

tips.content: Be extremely careful with signs! If you define UP as positive, then $a$ is $-9.81$, initial velocity $u$ is positive, and any displacement BELOW the launch point must be entered as a negative value.

questions.q: In the classic 'Monkey and Hunter' experiment, where should the hunter aim to hit a monkey that drops at the exact moment the rifle is fired?

opts.D: It depends on the speed of the bullet

questions.exp: The answer is C. The hunter should aim directly at the monkey. Both the bullet and the monkey experience the same vertical acceleration ($g$), so they 'fall' away from their inertial paths at the same rate.

questions.q: Why does aiming directly at the monkey work regardless of the bullet's speed?

opts.B: The monkey and bullet fall the same vertical distance from the aim-line in the same time
opts.C: The bullet travels in a straight line
opts.D: The air resistance cancels out the gravity

questions.exp: The answer is B. Without gravity, the bullet would hit the monkey's original position. With gravity, both drop by $1/2 gt^2$ from where they would have been, meaning they still meet.

questions.q: If the bullet travels faster, how does the collision point change?

opts.C: The collision point is the same

questions.exp: The answer is B. A faster bullet reaches the monkey's horizontal position in less time ($t$). Since distance fallen is $1/2 gt^2$, a smaller $t$ means they collide closer to the monkey's original height.

questions.q: What force acts on both the monkey and the bullet during their flight?
questions.exp: The correct answer is gravity (or weight). This is the only force considered in the basic model, causing both objects to accelerate downwards at $9.81 ms^{-2}$.

questions.q: Does the mass of the monkey affect the outcome of this experiment?

opts.B: Yes, lighter monkeys are easier to hit
opts.C: No, acceleration due to gravity is independent of mass
opts.D: Only if air resistance is high

questions.exp: The answer is C. In a vacuum (or ignoring air resistance), all objects accelerate at $g$ regardless of their mass. This is a fundamental principle of Galilean gravity.

questions.q: If the hunter aims directly at the monkey but the monkey does NOT fall, what happens?

opts.B: The bullet passes below the monkey
opts.C: The bullet passes above the monkey

questions.exp: The answer is B. If the monkey stays still, it doesn't drop. However, the bullet still follows a parabolic path and drops below the line of sight, missing the monkey.

questions.q: What is the shape of the bullet's path in this experiment?
questions.exp: The correct answer is a parabola. Like all projectiles with constant horizontal velocity and vertical acceleration, the path is parabolic.

questions.q: In a real-world scenario with significant air resistance, where should the hunter aim?
questions.exp: The answer is B. Air resistance slows the bullet down, so it takes longer to reach the monkey. Gravity has more time to act, so the bullet falls further than the monkey does in the same interval.

questions.q: The 'Monkey and Hunter' demonstrates which principle?

opts.B: Independence of horizontal and vertical motion

questions.exp: The answer is B. It shows that vertical acceleration ($g$) affects the vertical position of both objects identically, regardless of their different horizontal velocities.

questions.q: Which factors determine exactly *where* the collision occurs? (Select all that apply)
questions.exp: The correct options are A, B, and D. Speed and distance determine the time of flight ($t = d/v_x$), and height determines the starting position. Mass (C) does not affect the trajectory in the absence of air resistance.

tips.content: The Monkey and Hunter is the ultimate proof of $s = 1/2 gt^2$. No matter how fast the bullet goes, it always 'drops' away from the straight-line aim by that exact amount. Since the monkey also 'drops' by that amount from rest, they are guaranteed to meet.

title: Force, mass, acceleration and newton's second law

questions.q: What is the standard SI unit for Force?
questions.exp: The answer is C. Force is measured in Newtons ($N$), named after Sir Isaac Newton. $1 N$ is defined as the force needed to accelerate $1 kg$ at $1 ms^{-2}$.

questions.q: Which equation represents Newton's Second Law for a constant mass?
questions.exp: The answer is B. The resultant force acting on an object is equal to the mass of that object multiplied by its acceleration ($F = ma$).

questions.q: If the resultant force on an object is zero, what can be said about its motion?

opts.C: It is either at rest or moving at a constant velocity

questions.exp: The answer is C. This is Newton's First Law. Zero resultant force means zero acceleration, so the velocity remains constant (which includes $0 ms^{-1}$).

questions.q: Calculate the force required to accelerate a $0.5 kg$ mass at $4 ms^{-2}$.
questions.exp: The correct answer is $2 N$. Using $F = ma$, we get $0.5 kg \times 4 ms^{-2} = 2 N$.

questions.q: What happens to the acceleration of an object if the resultant force is doubled while the mass remains constant?
questions.exp: The answer is C. Since $a = F/m$, acceleration is directly proportional to the force. Doubling $F$ doubles $a$.

questions.q: What happens to the acceleration of an object if the mass is doubled while the resultant force remains constant?
questions.exp: The answer is A. Acceleration is inversely proportional to mass ($a \propto 1/m$). Doubling the mass makes it harder to accelerate, so $a$ is halved.

questions.q: An object of mass $10 kg$ has two forces acting on it: $50 N$ to the right and $20 N$ to the left. Calculate its acceleration.
questions.exp: The correct answer is $3 ms^{-2}$. Resultant force $F = 50 - 20 = 30 N$. Then $a = F/m = 30 / 10 = 3 ms^{-2}$.

questions.q: How is mass defined in physics?

opts.B: The amount of space an object takes up
opts.C: The measure of an object's resistance to acceleration (inertia)
opts.D: The force of gravity on an object

questions.exp: The answer is C. Inertial mass is a measure of how much an object resists a change in its motion. Weight (D) is a force ($W = mg$).

questions.q: A car of mass $1200 kg$ is braking with a force of $6000 N$. What is its acceleration?
questions.exp: The answer is B. $a = F/m = -6000 / 1200 = -5 ms^{-2}$. The negative sign indicates deceleration (slowing down).

questions.q: Which of the following are vector quantities? (Select all that apply)
questions.exp: The correct options are A, C, and D. Force, acceleration, and displacement all have both magnitude and direction. Mass (B) is a scalar quantity.

tips.content: In $F = ma$, the '$F$' refers specifically to the RESULTANT (or net) force. If there are multiple forces, you must resolve them into a single value before calculating acceleration. Always draw a free-body diagram to avoid missing forces like friction or air resistance.

questions.q: What is the definition of the moment of a force?

opts.A: Force multiplied by the distance moved.
opts.B: The product of the force and the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force.
opts.C: The sum of all forces acting on a body.
opts.D: The rate of change of momentum.

questions.exp: The answer is B. By definition, a moment is $M = F 	imes d$, where $d$ must be the perpendicular distance from the pivot point to the line along which the force acts.

questions.q: What is the SI unit for a moment?
questions.exp: The answer is C. Since a moment is force (Newtons) multiplied by distance (meters), the unit is Newton-meters ($Nm$).

questions.q: According to the principle of moments, what is required for a body to be in rotational equilibrium?

opts.A: The total upward force must equal the total downward force.
opts.B: The sum of the clockwise moments must equal the sum of the anticlockwise moments about any point.
opts.C: The net force acting on the body must be zero.
opts.D: The body must be moving at a constant velocity.

questions.exp: The answer is B. For rotational equilibrium specifically, the sum of clockwise moments must equal the sum of anticlockwise moments. Note that option C is required for translational equilibrium, but not specifically rotational.

questions.q: A $10\ N$ force is applied at an angle of $30^{\circ}$ to a door at a distance of $0.8\ m$ from the hinge. Calculate the moment.
questions.exp: The answer is C. The perpendicular distance is $0.8 	imes \sin(30^{\circ}) = 0.4\ m$. The moment is $10\ N 	imes 0.4\ m = 4.0\ Nm$.

questions.q: Where does the weight of a uniform object act from in a moments calculation?
questions.exp: The correct answer is the center of mass. For a uniform object, this is located at its geometric center. We treat the entire weight of the object as acting from this single point.

questions.q: A uniform plank of length $2.0\ m$ and weight $50\ N$ is supported at its center. A $20\ N$ weight is placed $0.5\ m$ from the left end. Where must a $30\ N$ weight be placed to balance it?

opts.A: $0.33\ m$ from the right of the center
opts.B: $0.5\ m$ from the right of the center
opts.C: $1.0\ m$ from the right of the center
opts.D: $0.75\ m$ from the right of the center

questions.exp: The answer is A. The pivot is at the center ($1.0\ m$ mark). The $20\ N$ weight is $0.5\ m$ from the pivot. Anticlockwise moment $= 20 	imes 0.5 = 10\ Nm$. For balance, $30 	imes d = 10$, so $d = 10/30 = 0.33\ m$.

questions.q: If a system is in 'total equilibrium', which conditions must be met?

opts.C: Both resultant force and resultant moment are zero.

questions.exp: The answer is C. Total equilibrium requires translational equilibrium (sum of forces $= 0$) AND rotational equilibrium (sum of moments $= 0$).

questions.q: A uniform beam $4\ m$ long is supported at both ends. Its weight is $200\ N$. Calculate the upward force at each support.
questions.exp: The correct answer is $100\ N$. Because the beam is uniform, the weight acts exactly in the middle. By symmetry, each support carries half the load ($200/2 = 100\ N$).

questions.q: Which of the following would increase the moment of a force about a pivot?

opts.A: Increasing the magnitude of the force.
opts.B: Moving the force closer to the pivot.
opts.C: Increasing the perpendicular distance from the pivot.
opts.D: Applying the force at a $90^{\circ}$ angle to the beam.

questions.exp: The correct options are A, C, and D. Moment is increased by higher force or distance. Applying it at $90^{\circ}$ maximizes the 'perpendicular' component compared to other angles.

questions.q: A bridge is supported by two pillars, P and Q. A car is parked closer to pillar P. Which statement is true?

opts.A: The force on P is equal to the force on Q.
opts.B: The force on P is greater than the force on Q.
opts.C: The force on Q is greater than the force on P.
opts.D: The moments about P are zero.

questions.exp: The answer is B. Taking moments about Q, the car's weight has a larger distance to Q than to P, meaning pillar P must provide a larger upwards force to balance the weight.

tips.content: When a force is applied at an angle $\theta$ to a lever arm, the perpendicular distance is $d \sin(\theta)$. Alternatively, you can resolve the force into a perpendicular component ($F \sin(\theta)$) and use the full distance. Both methods give the same result!

questions.q: What is a 'couple' in physics?

opts.A: Two forces acting in the same direction.
opts.B: A pair of equal and opposite forces acting along the same line.
opts.C: A pair of equal and parallel forces acting in opposite directions, separated by a distance.
opts.D: Any two forces that cause an object to rotate.

questions.exp: The answer is C. A couple consists of two forces of equal magnitude, acting in opposite directions, that are parallel but not collinear (displaced by a distance $s$).

questions.q: What is the resultant *force* of a couple?
questions.exp: The answer is C. Because the two forces are equal and opposite, they cancel out for translational motion ($F - F = 0$). A couple only produces rotation (torque).

questions.q: Which formula gives the torque of a couple?

opts.B: $2 	imes Force 	imes 	ext{distance between forces}$

questions.exp: The answer is A. The torque $T = F 	imes d$, where $F$ is the magnitude of one of the forces and $d$ is the perpendicular distance between the two forces.

questions.q: A driver applies a couple to a steering wheel of diameter $38\ cm$ using two $20\ N$ forces. Calculate the torque.
questions.exp: The answer is A. Convert diameter to meters: $0.38\ m$. Torque $= F 	imes d = 20\ N 	imes 0.38\ m = 7.6\ Nm$.

questions.q: Does the torque of a couple depend on the choice of pivot point?
questions.exp: The correct answer is No. A unique property of a couple is that its moment (torque) is the same about any point in its plane.

questions.q: A couple is applied to a rod. The forces are $15\ N$ each and the rod is $2\ m$ long. If the forces are applied at the very ends, what is the torque?
questions.exp: The answer is B. $T = F 	imes d = 15 	imes 2 = 30\ Nm$.

questions.q: Why does a couple not cause an object to accelerate linearly?

opts.A: Because the forces are too small.
opts.B: Because the resultant force is zero.
opts.C: Because the object is fixed to a pivot.
opts.D: Because torque only affects mass, not acceleration.

questions.exp: The answer is B. Newton's Second Law ($F=ma$) applies to the resultant force. Since the two forces in a couple are equal and opposite, the resultant is zero, so there is no linear acceleration.

questions.q: Calculate the force required to produce a torque of $50\ Nm$ with a separation of $25\ cm$.
questions.exp: The correct answer is $200\ N$. Convert $25\ cm$ to $0.25\ m$. $F = T / d = 50 / 0.25 = 200\ N$.

questions.q: Which of the following are examples of couples? (Select all that apply)

opts.B: Pushing a door open from one side.
opts.C: Turning a tap with two fingers on opposite sides.
opts.D: A cyclist pressing down on one pedal while the other moves up.

questions.exp: The correct options are A and C. These involve two equal and opposite forces. Pushing a door (B) is a single force. A cyclist (D) often applies different forces to the pedals, though it mimics a couple.

questions.q: If the distance between the two forces of a couple is doubled, but the torque remains the same, the magnitude of each force must:
questions.exp: The answer is C. Since $T = F 	imes d$, if $d$ is multiplied by $2$, $F$ must be multiplied by $0.5$ (halved) to keep $T$ constant.

tips.content: A common mistake is to multiply by two (doing $2 	imes F 	imes d$). Remember, the formula $T = Fd$ already accounts for both forces because each force $F$ acts at a distance $d/2$ from the center, so $(F 	imes d/2) + (F 	imes d/2) = Fd$.

questions.q: What is the definition of density?
questions.exp: The answer is B. Density ($\rho$) is defined as the ratio of an object's mass ($m$) to its volume ($V$).

questions.q: What is the SI unit for density?
questions.exp: The answer is C. Mass is measured in $kg$ and volume in $m^3$, so density is $kg/m^3$.

questions.q: Convert $1\ g/cm^3$ into $kg/m^3$.
questions.exp: The answer is C. There are $1,000\ g$ in a $kg$, and $1,000,000\ cm^3$ in a $m^3$. So, $1\ g/cm^3 = 0.001\ kg / 0.000001\ m^3 = 1,000\ kg/m^3$.

questions.q: Calculate the mass of a gold bar with volume $0.002\ m^3$. (Density of gold $= 19,300\ kg/m^3$)
questions.exp: The correct answer is $38.6\ kg$. Using $m = ho V = 19,300 	imes 0.002 = 38.6\ kg$.

questions.q: An alloy is made of two metals. Metal A has density $ho_A$ and volume $V_A$. Metal B has density $ho_B$ and volume $V_B$. What is the total density of the alloy?

opts.B: $ rac{ho_A V_A + ho_B V_B}{V_A + V_B}$
opts.D: $ rac{V_A + V_B}{ho_A V_A + ho_B V_B}$

questions.exp: The answer is B. Average density is Total Mass / Total Volume. Total mass is $m_A + m_B = ho_A V_A + ho_B V_B$. Total volume is $V_A + V_B$.

questions.q: A cube has sides of $2\ cm$ and a mass of $16\ g$. What is its density in $kg/m^3$?
questions.exp: The answer is A. Volume $= 2 	imes 2 	imes 2 = 8\ cm^3$. Density $= 16\ g / 8\ cm^3 = 2\ g/cm^3$. Converting to SI: $2 	imes 1,000 = 2,000\ kg/m^3$.

questions.q: What happens to the density of a gas if it is compressed to half its volume at a constant temperature?
questions.exp: The correct answer is that it doubles. Since $ho = m/V$, if $m$ stays constant and $V$ is halved, $ho$ must double.

questions.q: Which of the following objects will float in water (density $\approx 1,000\ kg/m^3$)?
questions.exp: The answer is B. An object floats if its density is less than water. $ho_B = 20 / 0.03 \approx 667\ kg/m^3$. All others have densities $\ge 1,000\ kg/m^3$.

questions.q: A sphere has radius $r$. If the radius is doubled, what happens to the density (assuming mass is constant)?
questions.exp: The answer is C. Volume of a sphere $V =  rac{4}{3}\pi r^3$. If $r$ doubles, $V$ increases by $2^3 = 8$. Since $ho = m/V$, the density becomes $1/8$ of the original.

questions.q: Calculate the volume in $m^3$ of $500\ kg$ of oil with a density of $850\ kg/m^3$.
questions.exp: The correct answer is $0.588\ m^3$. $V = m / ho = 500 / 850 \approx 0.5882... \ m^3$.

tips.content: To convert from $g/cm^3$ to $kg/m^3$, just multiply by $1000$. To go from $cm^3$ to $m^3$, you divide by $100^3$ (which is $1,000,000$), not just $100$. This is a very common source of calculation errors!

questions.q: What is the definition of pressure?
questions.exp: The answer is A. Pressure ($P$) is defined as the force ($F$) acting normally (perpendicularly) to a surface, divided by the area ($A$) of that surface.

questions.q: Which unit is equivalent to the Pascal ($Pa$)?
questions.exp: The answer is C. Since $P = F/A$, and force is in Newtons ($N$) and area in $m^2$, the unit is $N/m^2$.

questions.q: A person weighing $600\ N$ stands on one foot with an area of $0.02\ m^2$. What is the pressure exerted on the ground?
questions.exp: The answer is C. $P = F/A = 600 / 0.02 = 30,000\ Pa$ (or $30\ kPa$).

questions.q: Why do snowshoes prevent you from sinking into deep snow?

opts.A: They increase the weight of the person.
opts.B: They reduce the force acting on the snow.
opts.C: They increase the area over which the weight is spread, reducing pressure.
opts.D: They decrease the friction between the boots and the snow.

questions.exp: The answer is C. By increasing the area $A$ in the equation $P = F/A$, the pressure $P$ is reduced for the same weight $F$. Lower pressure prevents the snow from deforming and sinking.

questions.q: Calculate the force exerted on a window of area $2.5\ m^2$ if the air pressure is $100,000\ Pa$.
questions.exp: The correct answer is $250,000\ N$. $F = P 	imes A = 100,000 	imes 2.5 = 250,000\ N$.

questions.q: If the same force is applied to half the area, the pressure will be:
questions.exp: The answer is B. Pressure is inversely proportional to area. If $A$ becomes $A/2$, $P$ becomes $2P$.

questions.q: What is 'atmospheric pressure' at sea level approximately?
questions.exp: The answer is C. Standard atmospheric pressure is roughly $1.01 	imes 10^5\ Pa$, often simplified to $100\ kPa$ in exam questions.

questions.q: A force of $20\ N$ is applied to a piston with a circular face of radius $0.05\ m$. Calculate the pressure.
questions.exp: The correct answer is $2546\ Pa$. Area $A = \pi r^2 = \pi (0.05)^2 \approx 0.00785\ m^2$. $P = F/A = 20 / 0.00785 \approx 2546\ Pa$.

questions.q: Which of the following would increase the pressure exerted by an object on a surface?

opts.A: Adding more mass to the object.
opts.B: Sharpening the edge of the object.
opts.C: Laying the object on its largest face.
opts.D: Moving the object to the Moon.

questions.exp: The correct options are A and B. Adding mass increases force ($F=mg$), and sharpening reduces area. Laying it on a large face increases area (lowers pressure). Moving to the Moon reduces $g$, thus reducing weight and pressure.

questions.q: A hydraulic jack uses pressure. If a force $F_1$ is applied to a small area $A_1$, the pressure is transmitted to a larger area $A_2$. The force produced ($F_2$) will be:
questions.exp: The answer is C. Since $P = F_1/A_1 = F_2/A_2$, then $F_2 = F_1 	imes (A_2/A_1)$. Since $A_2 > A_1$, the output force is magnified.

tips.content: Always check your units for area! If the area is in $cm^2$, you must divide by $10,000$ to get $m^2$. If it's in $mm^2$, divide by $1,000,000$. Using $cm^2$ instead of $m^2$ is the most frequent reason for being off by several orders of magnitude.

questions.q: Which formula correctly gives the pressure $P$ at a depth $h$ in a fluid?
questions.exp: The answer is B. Hydrostatic pressure depends on the density of the fluid ($ho$), the gravitational field strength ($g$), and the depth ($h$).

questions.q: What happens to the pressure as you go deeper into a lake?
questions.exp: The answer is C. Because $P = ho gh$, pressure is directly proportional to depth ($h$).

questions.q: Calculate the pressure due to water at a depth of $10\ m$. ($ho_{water} = 1,000\ kg/m^3, g = 9.81\ N/kg$)
questions.exp: The answer is B. $P = ho gh = 1,000 	imes 9.81 	imes 10 = 98,100\ Pa$.

questions.q: Does the pressure at a certain depth in a still liquid depend on the shape of the container?

opts.A: Yes, wider containers have higher pressure.
opts.B: Yes, narrower containers have higher pressure.
opts.C: No, it only depends on depth and density.
opts.D: Yes, it depends on the total volume of liquid.

questions.exp: The answer is C. This is known as the hydrostatic paradox. The pressure at any point at a certain depth is the same regardless of the shape of the vessel.

questions.q: What is the total pressure at a depth $h$ in the ocean, considering the atmosphere?
questions.exp: The correct answer is $P_{atm} + ho gh$. The water pressure formula only gives the pressure *added* by the liquid. To find the absolute pressure, you must add the pressure from the air above the surface.

questions.q: An object is submerged in a fluid. Why is there an upward 'buoyant force' (upthrust)?

opts.A: Because the fluid is trying to escape.
opts.B: Because pressure at the bottom of the object is greater than at the top.
opts.C: Because the object is less dense than the fluid.
opts.D: Because the object's weight is zero in water.

questions.exp: The answer is B. Pressure increases with depth. Therefore, the bottom surface of an object experiences a larger upward force than the downward force on the top surface. The difference is upthrust.

questions.q: Calculate the depth in a pool of mercury ($ho = 13,600\ kg/m^3$) where the pressure is $100,000\ Pa$.
questions.exp: The correct answer is $0.75\ m$. $h = P / (ho g) = 100,000 / (13,600 	imes 9.81) \approx 0.75\ m$.

questions.q: A dam is built to hold back a lake. Why is the dam usually much thicker at the bottom than at the top?

opts.A: To save materials at the top.
opts.B: Because the water is colder at the bottom.
opts.C: Because the pressure of the water is greatest at the bottom.
opts.D: To prevent fish from swimming over.

questions.exp: The answer is C. Since $P = ho gh$, the pressure (and therefore the force per unit area) exerted by the water increases with depth. The dam must be stronger at the base to withstand this higher pressure.

questions.q: Which factors determine the upthrust on an object submerged in a liquid? (Select all that apply)

opts.B: The volume of the object submerged.

questions.exp: The correct options are A, B, and D. According to Archimedes' Principle, Upthrust = Weight of fluid displaced $= ho_{fluid} V_{submerged} g$. The object's own density only determines if it will sink or float, not the magnitude of the upthrust itself.

questions.q: If you take a balloon deep underwater, what happens to its volume?
questions.exp: The answer is B. As the depth increases, the external water pressure increases. This high pressure compresses the air inside the balloon, reducing its volume (Boyle's Law).

tips.content: Don't confuse the pressure formula $P = F/A$ with $P = ho gh$. $P = F/A$ is a general definition for solids and surfaces, while $P = ho gh$ is a derived formula specifically for the pressure within a column of fluid due to its own weight.

questions.q: What is the primary cause of upthrust on an object submerged in a fluid?

opts.A: The object's density compared to the fluid.
opts.B: The difference in pressure between the top and bottom of the object.
opts.C: The viscosity of the fluid resisting the object's weight.
opts.D: The surface tension of the fluid pushing upwards.

questions.exp: The answer is B. Pressure in a fluid increases with depth ($p = ho gh$). Because the bottom of a submerged object is at a greater depth than the top, it experiences a larger upward force from the fluid than the downward force at the top, resulting in a net upward force called upthrust.

questions.q: State Archimedes' Principle.
accepted_answers: The upthrust is equal to the weight of the fluid displaced
The upward buoyant force exerted on a body immersed in a fluid is equal to the weight of the fluid that the body displaces
questions.exp: The correct answer is that upthrust is equal to the weight of the fluid displaced. This applies to both partially and fully submerged objects.

questions.q: An object of volume $0.05 m^3$ is fully submerged in water (density $1000 kg m^{-3}$). Calculate the upthrust. (Use $g = 9.81 m s^{-2}$)
questions.exp: The answer is B. Upthrust $U = ho Vg$. So, $U = 1000 	imes 0.05 	imes 9.81 = 490.5 N$, which rounds to $491 N$.

questions.q: If an object is floating in equilibrium, what is the relationship between its weight and the upthrust acting on it?
questions.exp: The correct answer is Weight = Upthrust. For an object to float in equilibrium, the resultant force must be zero, meaning the upward buoyant force must exactly balance the downward gravitational force.

questions.q: A block floats in a liquid with $60\%$ of its volume submerged. What can be concluded about the density of the block compared to the liquid?

opts.A: The block's density is $60\%$ of the liquid's density.
opts.B: The block's density is $40\%$ of the liquid's density.
opts.C: The block's density is equal to the liquid's density.
opts.D: The block's density is $1.6$ times the liquid's density.

questions.exp: The answer is A. For floating objects, the fraction submerged is equal to the ratio of the object's density to the fluid's density ($ rac{ho_{object}}{ho_{fluid}} =  rac{V_{submerged}}{V_{total}}$).

questions.q: Which of the following factors affect the magnitude of upthrust on a fully submerged object? (Select all that apply)
questions.exp: The correct options are A and C. Upthrust is defined by $U = ho Vg$. It depends only on the fluid density and the volume of fluid displaced (which equals the object's volume if fully submerged). It does not depend on the object's mass or the depth (assuming the fluid is incompressible).

questions.q: A ship moves from a freshwater river (density $1000 kg m^{-3}$) into the saltwater ocean (density $1030 kg m^{-3}$). How does the submerged volume of the ship change?

opts.D: It depends on the ship's speed.

questions.exp: The answer is B. The ship's weight is constant, so the upthrust required to float remains the same. Since $U = ho Vg$, if the density $ho$ increases (saltwater), the volume displaced $V$ must decrease.

questions.q: What is the apparent weight of a $5 kg$ object that experiences $20 N$ of upthrust?
questions.exp: The answer is A. Weight $W = mg = 5 	imes 9.81 = 49.05 N$. Apparent weight = $W - U = 49.05 - 20 = 29.05 N$.

questions.q: Define 'apparent weight'.
accepted_answers: The weight of an object measured while submerged in a fluid
Normal contact force from a scale when submerged
questions.exp: The correct answer is Weight minus Upthrust. It represents the net downward force and is what a scale would read if the object was weighed while submerged.

questions.q: A sphere is submerged in oil. If the density of the oil is halved, what happens to the upthrust on the sphere?
questions.exp: The answer is C. Upthrust is directly proportional to the density of the fluid ($ho$). Halving the density while keeping volume constant halves the upthrust.

tips.content: When calculating upthrust, always remember that 'V' in $ho Vg$ is the volume of the *submerged* part of the object, not necessarily the total volume of the object itself.
A common exam trick is to ask if upthrust increases with depth. As long as the object is fully submerged and the fluid density is constant, upthrust remains the same regardless of depth!

questions.q: What is the fundamental definition of work done $W$ by a constant force $F$?
questions.exp: The answer is B. Work done is defined as the product of the force and the displacement in the direction of the force ($W = Fs$).

questions.q: State the unit for Work Done.
questions.exp: The correct answer is the Joule ($J$). One Joule is equal to the work done when a force of $1 N$ moves an object $1 m$.

questions.q: A force of $20 N$ is applied at an angle of $60^{\circ}$ to the horizontal to pull a crate $5 m$ along the ground. Calculate the work done.
questions.exp: The answer is C. Use $W = Fs \cos(	heta)$. So, $W = 20 	imes 5 	imes \cos(60) = 100 	imes 0.5 = 50 J$.

questions.q: How much work is done by the centripetal force on a satellite in a circular orbit?
questions.exp: The answer is A. Work is only done if there is displacement *in the direction* of the force. In circular motion, the force is perpendicular to the direction of travel ($\cos(90) = 0$), so no work is done.

questions.q: What does the area under a Force-displacement graph represent?
questions.exp: The correct answer is Work Done. For a constant force, it is a rectangle ($F 	imes s$). For a variable force, you must integrate or find the area of the shape.

questions.q: A $10 kg$ mass is lifted vertically $2 m$. What is the work done against gravity? (Use $g = 9.81 m s^{-2}$)
questions.exp: The answer is B. $W = Fs$. Here, the force required is the weight ($mg$). $W = (10 	imes 9.81) 	imes 2 = 196.2 J$.

questions.q: Work done is a ______ quantity.
questions.exp: The answer is B. Work is a scalar quantity because it is the dot product of two vectors (force and displacement) and does not have a direction.

questions.q: A car engine provides a constant driving force of $500 N$ to maintain a constant speed. How much work does the engine do over $1 km$?
questions.exp: The correct answer is $500,000 J$. Be careful with units! $1 km = 1000 m$. $W = 500 	imes 1000 = 500,000 J$.

questions.q: If the angle between the force and displacement is $180^{\circ}$, the work done is:
questions.exp: The answer is B. $\cos(180) = -1$. This occurs when the force opposes motion, such as friction doing negative work on a sliding object.

questions.q: Power is defined as the rate of doing work. If $100 J$ of work is done in $5 s$, what is the power?
questions.exp: The answer is B. $P = W/t = 100 / 5 = 20 W$.

tips.content: Always identify which component of the force is parallel to the motion. If the force is at an angle $	heta$ to the displacement, use $F \cos(	heta)$. Don't just multiply $F$ and $s$ blindly!

questions.q: What is the formula for kinetic energy $E_k$?
questions.exp: The answer is C. Kinetic energy is the energy an object possesses due to its motion, defined by $ rac{1}{2}mv^2$.

questions.q: Calculate the kinetic energy of a $0.5 kg$ ball moving at $10 m s^{-1}$.
questions.exp: The correct answer is $25 J$. $E_k = 0.5 	imes 0.5 	imes 10^2 = 0.25 	imes 100 = 25 J$.

questions.q: If the velocity of an object is doubled, by what factor does its kinetic energy increase?
questions.exp: The answer is B. Kinetic energy is proportional to the square of velocity ($E_k \propto v^2$). Doubling $v$ leads to $2^2 = 4$ times the energy.

questions.q: Which of the following is an alternative expression for kinetic energy in terms of momentum $p$?
questions.exp: The answer is B. Since $p = mv$, then $v = p/m$. Substituting into $E_k =  rac{1}{2}m(p/m)^2$ gives $p^2 / 2m$.

questions.q: A car's mass is $1200 kg$ and it has $600,000 J$ of kinetic energy. Calculate its speed (to 2 s.f.).
questions.exp: The correct answer is $31.6 m s^{-1}$ (rounded to $32$). $600,000 = 0.5 	imes 1200 	imes v^2 \Rightarrow 1000 = v^2 \Rightarrow v = \sqrt{1000} \approx 31.6 m s^{-1}$.

questions.q: In a perfectly elastic collision, which of the following is conserved?
questions.exp: The answer is C. By definition, an elastic collision is one where there is no loss of kinetic energy. Momentum is conserved in all closed-system collisions.

questions.q: An object has $100 J$ of kinetic energy. If its mass is doubled and its speed is halved, what is its new kinetic energy?
questions.exp: The answer is B. New $E_k =  rac{1}{2}(2m)(v/2)^2 =  rac{1}{2}(2m)(v^2/4) =  rac{1}{4}mv^2 =  rac{1}{2} (	ext{Original } E_k)$. $100 / 2 = 50 J$.

questions.q: The work done on an object by a net force is equal to the change in its ______.
questions.exp: The correct answer is Kinetic Energy. This is known as the Work-Energy Theorem ($W = \Delta E_k$).

questions.q: A $2 kg$ object is falling. At a certain point, it has $50 J$ of kinetic energy. What is its speed at this point?
questions.exp: The answer is B. $50 = 0.5 	imes 2 	imes v^2 \Rightarrow 50 = v^2 \Rightarrow v = \sqrt{50} \approx 7.07 m s^{-1}$.

questions.q: Kinetic energy is a ______ quantity.
questions.exp: The answer is A. Like work and all other forms of energy, kinetic energy has magnitude but no direction.

tips.content: Don't forget the square! A very common mistake is to forget to square the velocity in the $ rac{1}{2}mv^2$ formula. Always double-check your calculation steps.

questions.q: What is the formula for Gravitational Potential Energy ($E_p$) in a uniform gravitational field?
questions.exp: The answer is B. $E_p = mgh$, where $m$ is mass, $g$ is gravitational field strength, and $h$ is change in height.

questions.q: Define 'Potential Energy'.
accepted_answers: Energy due to position or configuration
The capacity to do work based on an object's state
questions.exp: The correct answer is stored energy or energy due to position. For gravitational potential energy, it specifically refers to the energy an object has because of its position in a gravitational field.

questions.q: A $2 kg$ book is moved from a shelf $1 m$ high to a shelf $2.5 m$ high. What is the gain in GPE? (Use $g = 9.81 m s^{-2}$)
questions.exp: The answer is C. $\Delta E_p = mg\Delta h = 2 	imes 9.81 	imes (2.5 - 1) = 2 	imes 9.81 	imes 1.5 = 29.43 J$.

questions.q: Elastic potential energy is stored in a stretched spring. If the spring constant is $k$ and extension is $\Delta L$, what is the formula?
questions.exp: The answer is C. Elastic potential energy $E =  rac{1}{2}F\Delta L$. Since $F = k\Delta L$, the formula becomes $ rac{1}{2}k(\Delta L)^2$.

questions.q: In the formula $E_p = mgh$, what is the standard unit for $g$?
questions.exp: The correct answer is $N kg^{-1}$ or $m s^{-2}$. In the context of potential energy, it is often thought of as the force per unit mass.

questions.q: If an object is moved horizontally at a constant height, the change in GPE is:
questions.exp: The answer is C. GPE depends on vertical height ($h$). Since there is no change in height ($\Delta h = 0$), there is no change in gravitational potential energy.

questions.q: An object of mass $m$ is at height $h$. If it is taken to the Moon (where $g$ is $1/6$ of Earth's), what happens to its GPE relative to the surface?
questions.exp: The answer is C. Since $E_p = mgh$ and $m$ and $h$ are constant, $E_p$ is directly proportional to $g$. If $g$ is $1/6$th, $E_p$ is $1/6$th.

questions.q: What is the GPE of a $500 g$ mass held $2 m$ above the ground? (Use $g = 9.81 m s^{-2}$)
questions.exp: The correct answer is $9.81 J$. Convert mass to $kg$: $0.5 kg$. $E_p = 0.5 	imes 9.81 	imes 2 = 9.81 J$.

questions.q: Potential energy can be negative. True or False?
questions.exp: The answer is A. Potential energy depends on a chosen 'zero point'. If you define the ground as zero, a hole in the ground would have negative GPE. In gravitational fields of planets, the zero point is often infinity, making all GPE values negative.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a form of potential energy?
questions.exp: The answer is C. Thermal energy is essentially the kinetic energy of the particles within a substance. Chemical, Nuclear, and Electrical are all forms of stored (potential) energy.

tips.content: Always specify your 'reference level'. $h$ is the vertical height above a point you define as zero. It doesn't matter where you put zero as long as you are consistent!

questions.q: State the Principle of Conservation of Energy.
accepted_answers: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred
Total energy in a closed system remains constant
Energy can change form but the total remains the same
questions.exp: The correct answer is that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred from one form to another. This is a fundamental law of physics.

questions.q: An object falls from rest from a height $h$. Ignoring air resistance, what is its speed $v$ just before hitting the ground?
questions.exp: The answer is C. By conservation of energy, Loss in GPE = Gain in $E_k$. $mgh =  rac{1}{2}mv^2 \Rightarrow gh =  rac{1}{2}v^2 \Rightarrow v = \sqrt{2gh}$.

questions.q: A pendulum is released from a height. At the lowest point of its swing, what form is all the energy in (assuming no friction)?
questions.exp: The answer is B. At the lowest point, $h=0$, so all GPE has been converted into kinetic energy. It is at its maximum speed here.

questions.q: A $2 kg$ mass is dropped from $20 m$. If air resistance does $100 J$ of work, what is the kinetic energy when it hits the ground? (Use $g = 9.81 m s^{-2}$)
questions.exp: The answer is B. Initial GPE = $mgh = 2 	imes 9.81 	imes 20 = 392.4 J$. Work done by friction is energy lost to the surroundings. Final $E_k = 	ext{Initial GPE} - 	ext{Work Done} = 392.4 - 100 = 292.4 J$.

questions.q: Define 'Efficiency' in terms of energy.
accepted_answers: Useful energy out / total energy in
The ratio of useful work to total energy expended
questions.exp: The correct answer is Useful output energy divided by Total input energy. It is often expressed as a percentage.

questions.q: A motor is $70\%$ efficient. If it is supplied with $1000 J$ of energy, how much energy is 'wasted' as heat?
questions.exp: The answer is B. If $70\%$ is useful, $30\%$ is wasted. $0.30 	imes 1000 = 300 J$.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of energy being dissipated?

opts.A: A ball speeding up as it falls.
opts.C: A brake pad heating up during use.

questions.exp: The answer is C. Dissipation refers to energy being transferred into non-useful forms (like heat or sound) that spread out into the surroundings.

questions.q: If a car's velocity triples, how much more work must the brakes do to stop it?
questions.exp: The correct answer is 9 times. Work done by brakes = Change in $E_k$. Since $E_k \propto v^2$, if $v$ is 3x larger, $E_k$ is 9x larger ($3^2$), requiring 9x the work.

questions.q: A ball is thrown upwards with $50 J$ of kinetic energy. At its peak, what is its GPE (ignoring air resistance)?
questions.exp: The answer is C. At the peak, the ball momentarily stops ($v=0$, so $E_k=0$). By conservation of energy, all the initial $E_k$ has been converted to GPE.

questions.q: Total energy is always conserved in a system that is:
questions.exp: The answer is B. A closed system is one where no energy or matter can enter or leave. In such a system, the total energy remains constant regardless of the internal changes.

tips.content: Conservation of energy is often the fastest way to solve mechanics problems! Before using SUVAT, check if you can just equate Initial Energy to Final Energy ($E_k + E_p = 	ext{constant}$).

questions.q: What does the principle of conservation of energy state?

opts.A: Energy can be created but not destroyed.
opts.B: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred from one form to another.
opts.C: Total energy in a system always increases over time.
opts.D: Mechanical energy is always conserved even in the presence of friction.

questions.exp: The answer is B. The law of conservation of energy states that the total energy of an isolated system remains constant; it is said to be conserved over time. Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; rather, it can only be transformed or transferred from one form to another.

questions.q: What is the formula for Gravitational Potential Energy ($E_p$)?
questions.exp: The answer is C. Gravitational Potential Energy is calculated as the product of mass ($m$), gravitational field strength ($g$), and the vertical height ($h$) change.

questions.q: An object of mass $2.0\,kg$ is dropped from a height of $10\,m$. What is its kinetic energy just before it hits the ground? (Assume $g = 9.81\,m\,s^{-2}$ and ignore air resistance).
questions.exp: The answer is C. By conservation of energy, $E_k(gain) = E_p(loss)$. $E_p = mgh = 2.0 	imes 9.81 	imes 10 = 196.2\,J$. All this potential energy converts to kinetic energy at the bottom.

questions.q: If an object's velocity is doubled, by what factor does its kinetic energy increase?
questions.exp: The answer is B. Kinetic energy is proportional to the square of velocity ($E_k =  rac{1}{2}mv^2$). Therefore, doubling $v$ results in $(2)^2 = 4$ times the $E_k$.

questions.q: A ball is thrown vertically upwards. At the highest point of its flight, what can be said about its kinetic energy?
questions.exp: The correct answer is zero. At the maximum height, the instantaneous velocity of the ball is $0\,m\,s^{-1}$, and since $E_k =  rac{1}{2}mv^2$, the kinetic energy must also be zero.

questions.q: In the presence of air resistance, what happens to the total mechanical energy ($E_k + E_p$) of a falling object?

opts.B: It increases as the object speeds up.
opts.C: It decreases as energy is transferred to the surroundings as heat.

questions.exp: The answer is C. Air resistance does work against the motion, converting some mechanical energy into thermal energy. This means the sum of $E_k$ and $E_p$ decreases over time.

questions.q: Calculate the speed of a $0.5\,kg$ mass that has $100\,J$ of kinetic energy.
questions.exp: The answer is B. $E_k =  rac{1}{2}mv^2 \Rightarrow 100 = 0.5 	imes 0.5 	imes v^2 \Rightarrow 100 = 0.25v^2 \Rightarrow v^2 = 400 \Rightarrow v = 20\,m\,s^{-1}$.

questions.q: Which of the following are scalar quantities? Select all that apply.
questions.exp: The correct options are A, B, and D. Energy (in all forms) and Work Done are scalars. Velocity is a vector as it includes direction.

questions.q: A pendulum swings from a height $h$. Ignoring friction, what is its maximum speed $v$ at the bottom of the swing?
questions.exp: The answer is B. $mgh =  rac{1}{2}mv^2$. The masses cancel out: $gh =  rac{1}{2}v^2$, so $v^2 = 2gh$ and $v = \sqrt{2gh}$.

questions.q: State the SI unit for energy.
questions.exp: The correct answer is the Joule ($J$). One Joule is equal to the work done when a force of one Newton moves an object one meter.

tips.content: When dealing with energy conservation, always identify the 'Initial' and 'Final' states. In a vacuum, $E_{p,initial} + E_{k,initial} = E_{p,final} + E_{k,final}$. This is often simplified to $mgh =  rac{1}{2}mv^2$ when starting from rest at a height.

questions.q: What is the definition of Power?

opts.A: The total amount of work done.
opts.C: The force applied over a distance.
opts.D: The energy stored in a system.

questions.exp: The answer is B. Power is defined as the rate at which work is done or the rate at which energy is transferred ($P = \Delta E / t$).

questions.q: What is the SI unit of Power?
questions.exp: The correct answer is the Watt ($W$). One Watt is defined as one Joule per second ($1\,J\,s^{-1}$).

questions.q: A motor does $3000\,J$ of work in $1$ minute. What is its power output?
questions.exp: The answer is C. $P = W/t$. Remember to convert time to seconds: $1\,minute = 60\,s$. $P = 3000 / 60 = 50\,W$.

questions.q: Which of the following is equivalent to 1 Watt?
questions.exp: The answer is B. Since $P = Energy/time$, the units are $J/s$. $1\,J = 1\,N 	imes 1\,m = 1\,kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}$. Dividing by seconds gives $kg\,m^2\,s^{-3}$.

questions.q: If an engine's power is doubled, how long does it take to do the same amount of work?
questions.exp: The answer is C. Power and time are inversely proportional for a constant amount of work ($t = W/P$). Doubling $P$ halves $t$.

questions.q: Write the formula for power in terms of force ($F$) and velocity ($v$).
questions.exp: The correct answer is $P = Fv$. This is derived from $P = W/t = (F 	imes s)/t$. Since $s/t = v$, then $P = Fv$.

questions.q: A car travels at a constant speed of $20\,m\,s^{-1}$ against a resistive force of $400\,N$. What is the power of the engine?
questions.exp: The answer is C. Using $P = Fv$, $P = 400 	imes 20 = 8000\,W$ (or $8\,kW$).

questions.q: Which of these are units of power? Select all that apply.
questions.exp: The correct options are A, B, and C. Option D is the unit for Energy/Work ($Joules$), not Power.

questions.q: An electric heater has a power rating of $2\,kW$. How much energy does it use in $2$ hours?
questions.exp: The answer is C. $\Delta E = P 	imes t$. $P = 2000\,W$, $t = 2 	imes 60 	imes 60 = 7200\,s$. $\Delta E = 2000 	imes 7200 = 14,400,000\,J = 14.4\,MJ$.

questions.q: A person of mass $70\,kg$ runs up a flight of stairs $5\,m$ high in $10\,s$. What is their average power output? (Use $g = 9.81\,m\,s^{-2}$)
questions.exp: The answer is B. Work done = gain in $E_p = mgh = 70 	imes 9.81 	imes 5 = 3433.5\,J$. $Power = Work/time = 3433.5 / 10 = 343.35\,W$.

tips.content: A very common mistake is forgetting to convert time to seconds. Always check if the time is given in minutes or hours and convert to SI units ($s$) before calculating Power in Watts.

questions.q: For a vehicle moving at a constant velocity $v$, what must the engine's motive force be equal to?
questions.exp: The answer is C. According to Newton's First Law, if velocity is constant, the resultant force must be zero. Therefore, the forward motive force must exactly balance the backward resistive forces.

questions.q: If power is constant, what happens to the available motive force as the velocity of a vehicle increases?
questions.exp: The correct answer is it decreases. From $P = Fv$, if $P$ is a constant maximum value, then $F$ is inversely proportional to $v$ ($F = P/v$).

questions.q: A cyclist develops $250\,W$ of power while moving at $10\,m\,s^{-1}$. What is the total resistive force acting on the cyclist?
questions.exp: The answer is B. Using $P = Fv$, $250 = F 	imes 10$, so $F = 250 / 10 = 25\,N$.

questions.q: Why does a car have a 'top speed' even when the engine is running at maximum power?

opts.A: The engine runs out of fuel.
opts.B: The resistive forces increase with speed until they equal the maximum motive force.
